# How to turn a long PDF contract into a plain-English summary in 5 minutes

> **In short:** Open any AI assistant that accepts PDF uploads, attach the file, and ask a few focused questions about deadlines, fees, and cancellation. You'll get a plain-English summary in minutes — but always read the original key clauses yourself, because AI summaries can miss important details.

Contracts hide the important parts deep in the small print: the auto-renewal clause, the 30-day cancellation window, the fee that "may apply" later. An AI assistant can pull all of that into a short, readable summary, but only if you ask the right questions. This guide shows the technique that works in any major AI assistant that accepts PDF uploads — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, Le Chat, and others.

## Before you start

- An AI assistant that can read PDF files you upload. Most major assistants do this on their free tier, but very long contracts (over roughly 100 pages) may need a paid plan. Check the upload limit on the assistant's pricing page if your document is unusually long.
- The contract itself, saved as a PDF on your computer or phone.
- About 10 minutes. The summary itself is fast; the careful read-through at the end takes a moment.
- A quiet moment to actually read what the assistant tells you.

## Step 1 — Start a fresh chat and upload the PDF

Open your AI assistant and begin a brand-new conversation. A clean slate gives you the cleanest answer — older chats can confuse what the assistant reads in the new document. Once the chat is open, look for a **paperclip**, **attachment**, or **plus icon** near the message box. Tap that, then choose the PDF from your files. Some assistants also let you drag and drop the file straight onto the chat window.

If you don't see a paperclip, look for a **+ icon** or a button labeled something like **Add files** or **Upload**. On phone apps the icon often hides inside a small menu at the side of the text box.

💬 Example: "I'm uploading a contract. Please don't analyze it yet — I'll ask my questions one at a time."

You'll know it worked when the file name appears above the message box (or as a small chip beside it) and the assistant confirms it can see the document. If nothing happens after 30 seconds, the file may be too large — check the assistant's file-size limit before assuming the tool is broken.

## Step 2 — Ask for a plain-English overview first

Before you drill into the details, ask the assistant to give you a one-paragraph summary of what the document is, who it's between, and what it covers. This grounds the rest of the conversation: once the assistant has the big picture in mind, its later answers tend to be more accurate. Type your question in the message box where the uploaded file is already attached, and press Enter or the send arrow.

If the answer is longer than a paragraph or feels like a sales pitch, ask it to "shorten to one paragraph and skip the legal jargon." If the assistant gives you only a vague intro, ask a follow-up: "What kind of contract is this — a service agreement, a lease, a sales contract, or something else?"

💬 Example: "In plain English, what is this document, who are the parties, and what is the main thing being agreed to?"

You'll know it worked when the assistant gives you back a short paragraph (3 to 6 sentences) that names the type of contract, the people or companies involved, and the core purpose. If any of those three is missing, ask one more focused question before moving on.

## Step 3 — Ask the three questions that actually matter

Now the real work. In the same chat, type three focused questions, one after another: **deadlines** (when does this start, when can I leave, when does it auto-renew), **fees** (what does it cost, what changes after the first period, what extra charges might apply), and **cancellation** (how do I end this, what's the notice period, what happens if I miss it). Ask all three in one message so the assistant can answer them together. Press Enter and wait — usually under a minute.

If the assistant answers only one of the three, send the missing questions in a fresh message. If the answer feels too short, ask "Please list every date, dollar amount, and cancellation step you can find in the document."

💬 Example: "From this contract, list: 1) every deadline or time limit I need to know, 2) every fee, charge, or price that might apply, and 3) exactly how I cancel, including any notice period. Use bullet points."

You'll know it worked when the assistant gives you a structured, easy-to-scan answer with three clear sections. If any answer is "I can't find that in the document," ask it to point to the page or section it looked at — sometimes the answer is there and the assistant missed it.

## Step 4 — Push for the things people forget to ask

Once you have the big three, push one more layer. Contracts hide risk in the small print: what happens if you miss a payment, who pays legal fees in a dispute, whether the company can change terms mid-contract, and which country's laws apply. Ask these as a follow-up message in the same chat. The assistant now has the document **and** your earlier answers in its context window (the conversation history it can refer to), so it can build on what it already told you.

If the assistant's answer feels generic, paste in the actual clause: "I'm looking at section 8.2. What does this mean in plain English, and what's the worst-case scenario for me?"

💬 Example: "What happens if I miss a payment, who covers legal fees in a dispute, can the company change the terms mid-contract, and which state's laws apply? Point me to the section for each."

You'll know it worked when the assistant points to specific sections or page numbers and explains each risk in a sentence a non-lawyer can follow. If it just says "this is a standard clause" without explaining the actual risk, ask "what's the worst that could happen to me, in concrete terms?"

## Step 5 — Ask for a one-page checklist you can save

Now ask the assistant to compress everything into a short, printable checklist you can keep next to the contract. A checklist is easier to skim than a long summary, and it's the format most people actually re-read later. Ask in the same chat — the assistant still has the document and your earlier conversation. The result should fit on one screen: action items, key dates, and money amounts, plain and short.

If the checklist comes back too long, ask it to "cut this to the 10 most important items I'd forget in six months."

💬 Example: "Summarize everything we just found into a one-page checklist I can save: dates I must remember, amounts I'll be charged, and the steps to cancel. Keep it under 15 lines."

You'll know it worked when you can copy the answer into a notes app and read it in under a minute. If the checklist still feels like a wall of text, ask the assistant to put each item on its own line with the date or amount in bold.

## Step 6 — Spot-check three sections in the original PDF

AI summaries are good, but they're not perfect. The assistant can misread a clause, skip a footnote, or paraphrase something in a way that changes the meaning. Before you rely on the summary, open the original PDF and read three things yourself: the **cancellation clause** (usually labeled "Termination"), the **fees section** (often "Fees," "Charges," or "Payment Terms"), and any **date or deadline** the assistant flagged. If those three match what the assistant told you, the rest of the summary is very likely accurate.

If you can't find the section the assistant mentioned, use the PDF's search function (Ctrl+F on a computer, or the magnifying glass icon in most phone PDF apps) and type a keyword from the clause. If something doesn't match, send a follow-up question: "Section X says something different — can you re-read and reconcile?"

💬 Example: "Cancellation clause says 30 days, fees say a charge after year one, and auto-renewal is 60 days before expiration — can you re-read sections 7, 9, and 12 and tell me if your summary matches?"

You'll know it worked when the three sections you read match the summary, and you feel comfortable either signing the contract or deciding not to. If anything is off, send the assistant the exact text and ask it to explain the difference — that's how you catch the small print that changes everything.

## Common mistakes

- **Asking one giant question.** A single "summarize this contract" prompt usually gives a vague, hard-to-scan answer. Splitting it into overview, the three big questions, the hidden risks, and a checklist gets you a result you can actually use.
- **Trusting the summary without checking.** AI assistants can misread clauses, especially around fees and dates. Always read the cancellation, fees, and deadline sections yourself before you sign. The summary is a map, not a replacement for the territory.
- **Letting a long chat get messy.** After 20 or 30 messages, the assistant can lose track of what it told you earlier. If the conversation gets long, copy the checklist into a new chat, re-upload the PDF, and start fresh. Cleaner chats give cleaner answers.
- **Skipping the free-tier limits.** Some assistants let you upload small files on the free plan but cap the size on paid plans. If your upload fails, check the assistant's file-size limit before assuming the tool is broken.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** Leasing a new apartment, renewing a phone plan, signing up for a gym membership — the same five-step question set works for any contract. Once you've done it twice, the second one takes about three minutes.
- **For your business or work:** Vendor agreements, client contracts, partnership letters, freelancer terms — all of these can be summarized the same way. The checklist step is especially useful when you need to brief a partner or a manager who hasn't read the document.
- **If you want to go further:** Try a second AI assistant on the same PDF and compare the two summaries. Two independent reads catch more than one — and they don't always agree on which clauses matter most. Just don't paste a confidential contract into a tool your company hasn't approved for outside use.

## Try it now

Pick the last contract you signed — apartment lease, phone plan, gym membership, anything with more than five pages. Upload it to your AI assistant and ask the three big questions from Step 3. Save the answer somewhere you can find it in six months, when the renewal notice arrives. You'll never read a long contract the same way again.
